title: Maxims And Barbs
part_subtitle: How to Philosophize with a Hammer
paragraphs: Psychology finds work for idle hands to do.* What? does that make psychology a—devil?
Even the bravest of us only rarely has the courage for what he actually knows...
To live alone you must be an animal or a god—says Aristotle.* He left out the third case: you must be both—a philosopher...
‘All truth is simple.’—Is that not a compound lie?*— I want, once and for all, not to know many things.—Wisdom sets limits even to knowledge.
You recover best in your wild nature from your unnaturalness, your intellectuality...

What? is man just one of God’s mistakes? Or is God just one of man’s? — From the Military School of Life.—Whatever does not kill me makes me stronger.* Everyone else helps those who help themselves. Principle of brotherly love.
Do not be cowardly towards your actions! Do not abandon them after the event!—Remorse is indecent.*
Can an ass* be tragic?—Perishing under a load you can neither bear nor shed?... The case of the philosopher.

If you have your why? for life, then you can get along with almost any how?—Man does not strive for happiness; only the English do that.* Man created woman—but from what? From a rib of his God*—of his ‘ideal’...

What? you are searching? you would like to multiply yourself by ten, by a hundred? you are looking for followers?—Look for zeros!*— Posthumous people—like me, for example—are less well understood than timely ones,* but better heard. More strictly: we are never understood —and hence our authority...

Among Women.—’Truth? Oh you don’t know truth! Isn’t it an attempt on all our pudeurs?*— That is the kind of artist I like, modest in his needs; he actually wants only two things: his bread and his art—panem et Circen*...
Anyone who cannot manage to invest his will in things at least invests them with a meaning: i.e. he believes there is already a will in them (principle of ‘belief).

What? you chose virtue and puffed-out chests, and at the same time are looking enviously at the advantages of the inconsiderate?—But with virtue one dispenses with ‘advantages’... (for an anti-Semite’s front door). The complete woman commits literature as she commits a little sin:* to try it out, in passing, looking round to see if anyone has noticed and so that someone will notice...
Put yourself only in situations where you are not allowed any false virtues and where instead, like the tightrope walker* on his rope, you either fall or stand—or get away...
‘Wicked people have no songs.’*—How come the Russians* have songs?
‘German spirit’:* for the last eighteen years* a contradiction in terms. To search for beginnings you turn into a crab. The historian looks backwards; in the end he even believes backwards.
Contentment protects you even from catching cold. Did any woman who knew she was well-dressed ever catch cold?—I am assuming she was scantily clad.
I mistrust all systematists and avoid them. The will to system is a lack of integrity.
People think woman is profound—why? because you can never get to the bottom of her. Woman is not even shallow.
If a woman has manly virtues you should run away from her; and if she has no manly virtues she runs away herself.

‘How many remorsels did the conscience have to bite on in former times? what good teeth did it have?—And today? what’s missing?’—a dentist’s question.* Rash actions are rarely one-offs. With the first rash action people always do too much. Which is precisely why they usually commit a second —when they do too little...

A worm squirms when it is trodden on.* Clever move. By doing so it reduces the probability of being trodden on again. In the language of morality: humility.— There is a hatred of lying and pretence which comes from a sensitive notion of honour; there is exactly the same sort of hatred which comes from
cowardice, in so far as lying is forbidden by a divine command. Too cowardly to lie...

How little it takes to be happy! The sound of bagpipes.—Without music life would be a mistake. The Germans even think of God as singing songs.* On ne peut penser et écrire qu’assis* (G. Flaubert).*—Now I’ve got you, you nihilist!* Sitting still is precisely the sin against the holy ghost. Only thoughts which come from walking have any value.

There are times when we are like horses, we psychologists, and get restive: we see our own shadows in front of us fluctuating up and down. The psychologist has to look away from himself to see anything at all. Do we immoralists* do virtue any harm?—Just as little as anarchists* do to princes. Only since these latter have been shot at have they been sitting tight on their thrones again. Moral: we must shoot at morality. You are running on ahead?—Are you doing it as a shepherd? or as an exception? A third case would be the runaway... First question for the conscience.
Are you genuine? or just a play-actor? A representative? or the actual thing represented?—Ultimately you are even just an imitation play-actor ... Second question for the conscience.

The disillusioned man speaks.—I was looking for great human beings; I only ever found the apes of their ideal.* Are you one who looks on? or who lends a hand?—or who looks away, sidles off? ... Third question for the conscience.
Do you want to go along with others? or go on ahead? or go off on your own?... You must know what you want and that you want. Fourth question for the conscience.

Those were steps for me; I climbed up by way of them—and so had to pass beyond them. But they thought I wanted to sit down and rest on them... What does it matter that I turn out to be right! I am too often right.— And he who laughs longest today also laughs last.
Formula for my happiness: a yes, a no, a straight line, a goal*...
